verse.text: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus through the will of God, and Timothy our brother, to the assembly of God that is in Corinth, together with all the holy ones who are in the whole of Achaia:
verse.note: The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and the Septuagint's word for Israel assembled before God. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. 'Assembly' is used throughout this translation so that the reader can see it is one Greek word.

The word is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint's language for Israel. 'Saints', which many translations keep, now suggests canonised individuals or people of unusual virtue. Others render it 'God's people'.

verse.text: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort,
verse.note: The Greek noun and its verb occur ten times in verses 3 to 7 and cover comfort, encouragement and strengthening appeal. The traditional 'comfort' is kept throughout the passage so that the repetition is audible. It should be heard as active strengthening as well as consolation, and some translations prefer 'encouragement'.

verse.text: who comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those in any affliction through the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God.
For just as the sufferings of Christ overflow to us, so also through Christ our comfort overflows.
If we are afflicted, it is for your comfort and salvation; if we are comforted, it is for your comfort, which is at work in the endurance of the same sufferings that we also suffer,
and our hope for you is firm, since we know that as you are sharers in the sufferings, so also in the comfort.
For we do not want you to be unaware, brothers and sisters, of the affliction that came upon us in Asia: we were weighed down beyond measure, beyond our strength, so that we despaired even of living.
verse.note: The Greek plural was the normal way to address a mixed group of men and women, and Paul is writing to the whole community. 'Brothers' is the traditional rendering, and many recent translations have 'brothers and sisters' for the same reason.

This is the Roman province of Asia in the west of modern Turkey, whose leading city was Ephesus, not the continent. What happened to Paul there is not known. Suggestions include mob violence, imprisonment or a grave illness.

verse.text: Indeed, we ourselves have had the sentence of death within ourselves, so that we would not rely on ourselves but on God, who raises the dead.
He rescued us from so great a death, and he will rescue us; on him we have set our hope that he will rescue us yet again,
as you also join in helping us by your prayer, so that from many people thanks may be given on our behalf for the gift granted to us through many.
verse.note: The Greek is literally 'from many faces', which may simply mean 'persons' or may picture faces turned upward in prayer. The sentence is also loosely built. 'Through many' may go with the gift, as here (granted in answer to the prayers of many), or with the thanksgiving (thanks given by many).

verse.text: For this is our boast: the testimony of our conscience that we have conducted ourselves in the world, and all the more toward you, with holiness and sincerity from God, not by fleshly wisdom but by the grace of God.
verse.note: The manuscripts are divided between 'holiness' (hagiotēti) and 'simplicity' or 'straightforwardness' (haplotēti), two words that look very alike in Greek. SBLGNT reads 'holiness' and is followed here. Many translations and commentators prefer the other reading as better suited to the context, and the question remains open.

verse.text: For we are writing you nothing other than what you read and indeed understand, and I hope that you will understand completely,
verse.note: The Greek phrase can mean 'to the end' (in time, until the day of the Lord) or 'fully'. The contrast with 'in part' in the next verse favours 'completely', but both senses may be in play. The verbs 'read' and 'understand' also sound alike in Greek, a wordplay English cannot reproduce.

verse.text: just as you have also understood us in part: that we are your boast, just as you are ours, on the day of our Lord Jesus.
With this confidence I wanted to come to you first, so that you might have a second favor,
verse.note: The word is the one translated 'grace' elsewhere in the chapter; here it means the kindness or benefit of a visit. 'Second' most likely refers to the two visits planned in verse 16, one on the way to Macedonia and one on the way back. Some manuscripts read 'joy' in place of 'favor'.

verse.text: and to go on by way of you to Macedonia, and to come back to you from Macedonia and be sent on my way by you to Judea.
So when I wanted this, I was not being fickle, was I? Or do I make my plans according to the flesh, so that with me there is both Yes, yes and No, no?
verse.note: In Paul 'flesh' often means human nature left to itself, with its ordinary self-interested motives, not the body or sensuality in particular. The question is whether he plans as people usually do, saying yes and no as it suits him. 'Fleshly wisdom' in verse 12 has the same sense.

verse.text: But as surely as God is faithful, our word to you is not Yes and No.
For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was proclaimed among you through us, through me and Silvanus and Timothy, did not become Yes and No; rather, in him it has become Yes.
For however many the promises of God are, in him is the Yes. That is why through him also the Amen is spoken by us to the glory of God.
Now the one who makes us firm, together with you, in Christ, and who anointed us, is God,
verse.note: The Greek plays on two related words: God makes believers firm in Christos ('the Anointed One') and has 'anointed' (chrisas) them. 'Makes firm', 'sealed' and 'down payment' in verses 21 and 22 were all also terms used in commercial and legal transactions for guaranteeing a deal.

verse.text: who also sealed us and gave the Spirit in our hearts as a down payment.
verse.note: The word is a commercial term, borrowed from Semitic, for a first payment that secures a transaction and obliges the payer to pay the rest. 'Down payment' is the nearest modern equivalent; the older 'earnest' is no longer understood, and 'guarantee' loses the idea that part has already been paid. The Spirit is itself the payment: literally 'the down payment of the Spirit'.

verse.text: But I call on God as witness, on my own life, that it was to spare you that I did not come again to Corinth.
Not that we lord it over your faith; rather, we are fellow workers for your joy, for by faith you stand firm.
For I decided this for myself: not to come to you again in grief.
verse.note: The Greek noun and its verb occur eight times in verses 1–7 and are rendered 'grief' and 'grieve' throughout so that the repetition can be heard. 'Again' most naturally implies that Paul had already made one distressing visit to Corinth, which Acts does not record. Most scholars place this visit between the writing of 1 Corinthians and this letter.

verse.text: For if I grieve you, then who is there to make me glad except the one who is grieved by me?
And I wrote this very thing so that when I came I would not have grief from those who ought to have given me joy, being confident about all of you that my joy is the joy of you all.
verse.note: Paul refers to an earlier letter written 'through many tears' (verse 4). Older interpreters identified it with 1 Corinthians; most scholars today think it was a separate letter, sent after the distressing visit, that has not survived. A minority hold that part of it is preserved in chapters 10–13 of this letter.

verse.text: For I wrote to you out of great distress and anguish of heart, through many tears, not so that you would be grieved, but so that you would know the love I have for you, which is greater than you realize.
But if anyone has caused grief, it is not me he has grieved but, in some measure—not to press the point too hard—all of you.

note.term: in some measure—not to press the point too hard—all of you
note.traditional: but in part: that I may not overcharge you all

verse.note: The Greek is compressed and can be punctuated in more than one way. The verb means 'to weigh down, burden'; here it is taken as Paul declining to overstate the case, which is the majority view. Others read it as 'not to be too hard on him', and the older English tradition construed the sentence as 'he has grieved me only in part, so that I may not burden you all'.

verse.text: This penalty imposed by the majority is sufficient for such a person,
verse.note: Paul does not name the offender or the offence. The traditional view identified him with the man living with his father's wife in 1 Corinthians 5; most scholars now think he was someone who personally wronged or defied Paul during the distressing visit. 'The majority' may imply that a minority dissented, though the phrase can also mean simply the congregation as a body.

verse.text: so that now, on the contrary, you should rather forgive and comfort him, so that such a person is not swallowed up by excessive grief.
Therefore I urge you to confirm your love for him.
verse.note: The verb was used for formally ratifying a decision, will or agreement. Paul is probably asking for a public act by the congregation that restores the man, matching the formal penalty of verse 6, not merely for warmer private feelings.

verse.text: For this is also why I wrote: to find out whether you would stand the test, whether you are obedient in everything.
Anyone you forgive anything, I forgive too. For indeed what I have forgiven, if I have forgiven anything, has been for your sake in the presence of Christ,
verse.note: Literally 'in the face of Christ'. Most modern interpreters take this to mean 'before Christ, with Christ as witness'. The older rendering 'in the person of Christ', meaning as Christ's representative, is possible but less likely by the usage of the period.

verse.text: so that we are not taken advantage of by Satan, for we are not ignorant of his schemes.
When I came to Troas for the good news of Christ, and though a door had been opened for me in the Lord,
verse.note: The Greek word meant an announcement of good news, such as a victory or a ruler's accession, and a first-century reader heard it that way. 'Gospel' is the traditional English equivalent but now suggests a religious genre or a book. Several modern translations also use 'good news'. The phrase 'for the good news' here means 'to proclaim it'.

verse.text: I had no relief in my spirit, because I did not find my brother Titus. Instead I said farewell to them and went on to Macedonia.
But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumphal procession in Christ and through us reveals the scent of the knowledge of him in every place.
verse.note: The verb refers to the Roman triumph, the parade in which a victorious general displayed his captives and spoils through the city. With a personal object it normally means to lead someone as a captive in that parade, so Paul is most likely picturing himself as God's conquered prisoner on display. The older rendering 'causes us to triumph' lacks support in period usage; some scholars soften the image to 'makes a public display of us'.

verse.text: For we are Christ's fragrance to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing,
verse.note: Two words are distinguished here: 'scent' (a smell of any kind) in verses 14 and 16, and 'fragrance' (a pleasant smell) in this verse. Together they form the Septuagint's standard phrase for a sacrifice whose smell pleases God. Many scholars also see an allusion to incense burned along the route of a triumphal procession, though this is uncertain.

verse.text: to the one a scent from death to death, to the other a scent from life to life. And who is sufficient for these things?
For we are not, like so many, peddling the word of God; but from sincerity, as from God and in the sight of God, we speak in Christ.
verse.note: The verb comes from the word for a small retailer or tavern-keeper, a trade with a reputation for watering the wine and cheating on measures. It was a stock insult aimed at teachers who sold philosophy for profit. It thus carries both ideas: trading in the message for gain and adulterating it in the process.

verse.text: Are we beginning to commend ourselves again? Or do we need, as some do, letters of commendation to you or from you?
verse.note: Travellers in the ancient world commonly carried a letter from a known person vouching for them to strangers. Paul's rivals at Corinth seem to have arrived with such letters. 'Commendation' is used to keep the Greek's echo of 'commend ourselves' in the same verse.

verse.text: You yourselves are our letter, written on our hearts, known and read by all people.
verse.note: A few manuscripts read 'your hearts', and some translations have followed them because it seems to suit the image better. 'Our hearts' has much the stronger manuscript support and is the reading translated here.

verse.text: You show that you are a letter from Christ, delivered by us, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets that are hearts of flesh.
verse.note: The Greek verb means to serve or carry out a task for someone, and it belongs to the same word-family as 'servants' (v. 6) and 'service' (vv. 7–9). In the letter image it may mean that Paul carried the letter, or that he acted as Christ's scribe in producing it. 'Delivered' is chosen, but 'prepared by us' or 'cared for by us' are also possible.

The stone tablets are those of the law given to Moses at Sinai (Exodus 31:18). 'Hearts of flesh' echoes Ezekiel's promise that God would replace his people's heart of stone with a heart of flesh and put his Spirit in them (Ezekiel 36:26–27). Jeremiah's promise of a new covenant written on hearts (Jeremiah 31:31–33) lies behind verse 6.

verse.text: Such is the confidence we have through Christ toward God.
Not that we are competent in ourselves to count anything as coming from ourselves; rather, our competence is from God,
who also made us competent as servants of a new covenant, not of the written text but of the Spirit; for the written text kills, but the Spirit gives life.
verse.note: The traditional 'the letter kills' uses 'letter' in the sense of something written, but in this chapter English 'letter' already stands for a different Greek word meaning an epistle (vv. 1–3). The Greek word here means writing or a written document, and refers to the law as a text inscribed on stone (v. 7). The contrast is between a covenant that exists as writing and one given by the Spirit, not between literal and figurative interpretation, though that reading has a long history.

verse.text: Now if the service of death, carved in writing on stones, came with glory, so that the sons of Israel could not gaze at the face of Moses because of the glory of his face, a glory that was being set aside,
verse.note: The Greek noun belongs with the word rendered 'servants' in verse 6 and means the carrying out of a task for someone. 'Ministry' is the usual rendering, but it now suggests a church office and hides the link. 'The service of death' means the service whose outcome was death; the same pattern runs through 'of the Spirit', 'of condemnation' and 'of righteousness'.

Many translations say the glory on Moses' face was 'fading'. The Greek verb does not mean to fade; in the usage of the period, and everywhere else in Paul, it means to nullify, abolish or put out of operation. The same verb recurs in verses 11, 13 and 14 and is rendered the same way each time. Some scholars defend 'fading' as a contextual sense, but there is little lexical support for it.

verse.text: how will the service of the Spirit not come with glory all the more?
For if there was glory in the service of condemnation, much more does the service of righteousness overflow with glory.
Indeed, in this respect what had been glorified has not been glorified at all, on account of the glory that surpasses it.
For if what was being set aside came through glory, much more is what remains in glory.
Having such a hope, then, we act with great openness,
verse.note: The Greek word means frank, unconcealed speech or conduct, the freedom to say everything openly. 'Boldness' is the usual rendering and is not wrong. Here, though, the contrast is with Moses veiling his face, so the point is that nothing is hidden, not that Paul is courageous.

verse.text: and not like Moses, who used to put a veil over his face so that the sons of Israel would not gaze at the end of what was being set aside.
verse.note: The Greek word can mean a termination or a goal. On the first reading, the veil kept Israel from seeing the glory come to its end; on the second, it kept them from seeing what the passing covenant was aiming at, namely Christ. Both are defended by scholars; 'end' can carry either sense in English and is kept.

verse.text: But their minds were hardened. For to this very day the same veil remains at the reading of the old covenant, not lifted, because it is in Christ that it is set aside.
verse.note: This is the earliest known use of the phrase. Paul means the covenant made at Sinai as it was read aloud from the books of Moses in the synagogue, as verse 15 shows. It was not yet a title for a collection of books.

note.term: not lifted, because it is in Christ that it is set aside
note.traditional: remains unlifted, because only through Christ is it taken away

verse.note: The Greek can also be read: 'the same veil remains, it not being unveiled that in Christ it is set aside', where 'it' is the old covenant and not the veil. The rendering here follows the majority of translations in taking the veil as what is set aside. The word for 'lifted' is the verb rendered 'unveiled' in verse 18.

verse.text: Indeed, to this day, whenever Moses is read, a veil lies over their heart.
But whenever anyone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away.

note.traditional: when one turns to the Lord

verse.note: The Greek verb has no stated subject: it could be 'anyone', 'their heart' (v. 15), Israel, or Moses himself. The sentence adapts Exodus 34:34, where Moses removed his veil whenever he went in before the Lord, and Paul applies it to anyone who turns to the Lord now. Whether 'the Lord' here is God, as in Exodus, or Christ is debated.

verse.text: Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.
And we all, with unveiled face, seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are being transformed into the same image, from glory to glory, as from the Lord, the Spirit.

note.term: seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror

verse.note: The Greek verb, which is rare, is built on the word for mirror and can mean either to look at something in a mirror or to reflect as a mirror does. Most interpreters and the ancient versions favour 'seeing', which fits the contrast with those who could not look. 'Reflecting the glory of the Lord' would fit the comparison with Moses' shining face, and some translations adopt it.

note.traditional: the Spirit of the Lord / the Lord who is the Spirit

verse.note: The Greek is two nouns side by side, literally 'from Lord, Spirit'. It can be read as 'the Lord who is the Spirit' (in line with v. 17), 'the Spirit of the Lord', or 'the Lord of the Spirit'. The rendering leaves the two terms side by side as the Greek does; the first reading is the most widely held.

verse.text: For this reason, since we have this ministry as people who were shown mercy, we do not lose heart.

Rather, we have renounced the shameful, hidden things; we do not walk in cunning or tamper with the word of God, but by the open display of the truth we commend ourselves to every person’s conscience in the sight of God.
And even if our good news is veiled, it is veiled among those who are perishing,
verse.note: The Greek word was an ordinary term for the announcement of good news, used also of imperial proclamations. 'Gospel' has become a religious term or a book title, so the plainer rendering is used. Many modern translations alternate between the two.

verse.text: among whom the god of this age has blinded the minds of the unbelievers, so that they do not see the light of the good news of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God.
verse.note: The Greek word means an age or era, not the physical world. Paul shares the Jewish contrast between the present age and the age to come. Nearly all interpreters take the phrase to refer to Satan, as the power that holds sway in the present age. A few ancient interpreters took it to mean God himself.

note.traditional: lest the light ... should shine unto them

verse.note: The verb can mean either 'see clearly' or 'shine'. On the second reading the clause means 'so that the light of the good news does not shine on them', as in older English versions. Most modern translations take it as 'see', which fits the image of blinded minds.

verse.text: For we do not proclaim ourselves, but Christ Jesus as Lord, and ourselves as your slaves for Jesus’s sake.
verse.note: The word denotes a slave, a person owned by another, not a hired servant. Traditional versions soften it to 'servants'. Paul sets the word deliberately against 'Lord': Jesus is the master, and his envoys are at the Corinthians' disposal on his account.

verse.text: For it is the God who said, “Out of darkness light will shine,” who has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Christ.
verse.note: This is not an exact quotation of any one passage. It recalls God's command at creation, 'Let there be light' (Genesis 1:3), and may also echo Isaiah 9:2, where light shines on those living in darkness. Paul presents the coming of the good news as a new act of creation.

note.traditional: in the face of Jesus Christ

verse.note: Many manuscripts read 'Jesus Christ' here, and some 'Christ Jesus'. The edition translated reads simply 'Christ'. The meaning is not affected.

verse.text: But we have this treasure in clay jars, so that the surpassing greatness of the power may be God’s and not from us.
verse.note: Fired-clay pottery was the cheap, everyday container of the ancient world, easily broken and thrown away when damaged. The contrast is between the worth of the contents and the fragility of the container. The container is the messengers themselves in their bodily weakness.

verse.text: We are afflicted in every way but not crushed, at a loss but not at a total loss,

note.term: at a loss but not at a total loss

verse.note: The Greek plays on two forms of the same verb, the second strengthened by a prefix. The traditional rendering gives the sense but uses two unrelated words. The rendering here keeps the wordplay.

verse.text: persecuted but not abandoned, struck down but not perishing,
always carrying around in the body the dying of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be displayed in our body.
For we who live are constantly being handed over to death for Jesus’s sake, so that the life of Jesus may also be displayed in our mortal flesh.
So then, death is at work in us, but life in you.
But since we have the same spirit of faith, in keeping with what is written, “I believed, therefore I spoke,” we also believe, and therefore we also speak,
verse.note: The phrase may mean a disposition of faith, the same attitude as the psalmist's. It may instead refer to the Holy Spirit as the one who produces faith, in which case 'Spirit' would be capitalised. Interpreters are divided; the lower-case rendering follows most translations.

The quotation is from Psalm 116:10, in the wording of the ancient Greek translation, where it is numbered Psalm 115:1. The Hebrew text of that line is difficult and is usually translated differently. The psalm is a thanksgiving by someone rescued from death, which suits Paul's argument here.

verse.text: knowing that the one who raised Jesus will raise us also with Jesus and will present us together with you.
For all of this is for your sake, so that grace, increasing through more and more people, may make thanksgiving overflow to the glory of God.

note.term: increasing through more and more people

verse.note: The Greek word order allows 'through more and more people' to go with either verb. Either grace increases as it reaches more people, or grace, having increased, makes thanksgiving overflow through the many who give thanks. The Greek also plays on 'grace' and 'thanksgiving', and on 'increase' and 'more', which are related words.

verse.text: Therefore we do not lose heart. Even if our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day.
For the momentary lightness of our affliction is producing for us, beyond all measure, an eternal weight of glory,
verse.note: Paul sets 'momentary' against 'eternal' and 'lightness' against 'weight'. Many scholars think the image of glory as heavy reflects Hebrew, in which the word for 'glory' comes from a root meaning 'to be heavy'. This is plausible for a bilingual writer but cannot be proved.

verse.text: as we fix our eyes not on the things that are seen but on the things that are not seen. For the things that are seen are temporary, but the things that are not seen are eternal.
For we know that if our earthly house, this tent, is taken down, we have a building from God, a house not made by hands, eternal, in the heavens.

note.traditional: our earthly house of this tabernacle; the earthly tent we live in

verse.note: The Greek is literally 'our earthly house of the tent', meaning the house that is a tent. 'Tent' was a familiar image for the human body as a temporary dwelling, and Paul contrasts it with a permanent building from God. The verb 'taken down' is the ordinary word for striking a tent or demolishing a building, used here for death.

verse.text: For in this tent we groan, longing to be clothed over with our dwelling from heaven,

note.traditional: in this (tent) we groan; meanwhile we groan

verse.note: The Greek says only 'in this'. Most translations supply 'tent' or 'house' from verse 1, as here, and verse 4 supports that. The phrase can also be an idiom meaning 'for this reason' or 'meanwhile'.

note.traditional: clothed upon; to put on; be clothed with

verse.note: The verb means to put one garment on over another, and Paul sets it against plain 'unclothed' in verse 4. Most interpreters take the point to be that he would prefer to receive the heavenly body over the present one at Christ's coming, without first passing through death. How the 'naked' state of verse 3 relates to this is disputed.

verse.text: if indeed, once clothed, we will not be found naked.

note.traditional: being clothed; having put it on

verse.note: Most manuscripts read 'having put on (clothing)', which is followed here. A few witnesses read 'having taken off', giving 'even when unclothed we will not be found naked'. Some critical editions prefer that reading as the less obvious one. The difference is a single letter in Greek.

verse.text: For we who are in the tent groan, weighed down, because we do not want to be unclothed but to be clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.
The one who prepared us for this very thing is God, who gave us the Spirit as a down payment.
verse.note: The word is a commercial term for a first instalment that secures a transaction and commits the payer to the rest. 'Down payment' keeps both ideas: the Spirit is a real part of what is to come and a commitment to the remainder. 'Guarantee' and 'pledge', used in many versions, convey the assurance but not the part-payment.

verse.text: So we are always confident, and we know that while we are at home in the body we are away from the Lord—
for we walk by faith, not by what is seen—
verse.note: The traditional 'not by sight' takes the word as the act of seeing. In the usage of the period it normally means the visible form or appearance of a thing, that is, the thing seen. This fits the contrast just drawn in 4:18 between things seen and things unseen. Many commentators accept this sense, though some lexicons allow 'sight' here and most translations keep it.

verse.text: we are confident, I say, and would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord.
That is why we make it our ambition, whether at home or away, to be pleasing to him.
For all of us must be laid open before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive back for the things done through the body, according to what each has done, whether good or bad.
verse.note: Most translations have 'we must all appear'. The verb means to be made visible or disclosed, not merely to turn up, and Paul uses the same verb twice in verse 11 of his life being open to God and to the Corinthians. One rendering is used for all three so the link can be heard.

The word names the raised platform from which a Roman magistrate heard cases. Corinth had one in its forum, and according to Acts 18:12 Paul himself was brought before the proconsul Gallio there. The Corinthians would have pictured a concrete place.

verse.text: Knowing, then, the fear of the Lord, we persuade people; but to God we are laid open, and I hope we are laid open to your consciences as well.

We are not recommending ourselves to you again, but giving you an opportunity to boast on our behalf, so that you may have an answer for those who boast in what shows on the face and not in what is in the heart.
For if we were out of our minds, it was for God; if we are in our right mind, it is for you.
For the love of Christ holds us in its grip, since we have reached this judgment: one died for all, and so all died.

note.traditional: the love of Christ constraineth us; compels us; controls us

verse.note: The phrase can mean Christ's love for us or our love for Christ. Most interpreters take it as Christ's love, shown in the death the verse goes on to mention. The verb means to hold fast or hem in, and versions vary between 'compels', 'controls' and 'constrains'.

verse.text: And he died for all so that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for the one who died for them and was raised.
So from now on we know no one by human standards. Even though we once knew Christ by human standards, we now know him that way no longer.

note.traditional: according to the flesh; after the flesh

verse.note: The Greek is literally 'according to flesh', a Pauline phrase for the merely human way of measuring things. It describes the manner of knowing, not Christ himself. Paul is not dismissing knowledge of the earthly Jesus but an estimate of him, and of anyone, by outward criteria. Several modern versions translate similarly.

verse.text: So if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation: the old things have passed away; look, new things have come.

note.traditional: he is a new creature; he is a new creation

verse.note: The Greek has no verb, only 'if anyone in Christ, new creation'. It can mean that the person is a newly created being, the traditional reading, or that for such a person the new creation promised by the prophets has arrived. The wider wording about old things and new things favours the second, and many recent translations and commentators take it so. Some later manuscripts read 'all things have become new' at the end of the verse.

verse.text: And all of this is from God, who reconciled us to himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation;
that is, in Christ God was reconciling the world to himself, not counting their offenses against them, and he has entrusted to us the message of reconciliation.

note.traditional: God was in Christ, reconciling the world unto himself

verse.note: The words can be divided in two ways. One is 'God was in Christ, reconciling the world', a statement about God's presence in Christ. The other, followed here and by most recent translations, is 'in Christ God was reconciling the world', a statement about what God did through him. The grammar permits both, but the context concerns the act of reconciliation.

The word means a false step or lapse, and so a wrong done against someone. 'Trespasses' is the traditional rendering, but in current English it suggests entering property unlawfully. Some versions simply have 'sins', which hides the fact that Paul uses a different word here from the one in verse 21.

verse.text: So we are ambassadors on Christ's behalf, as God makes his appeal through us. We plead on Christ's behalf: be reconciled to God.
For our sake he made the one who knew no sin to be sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.
verse.note: Paul's wording is deliberately stark and is translated literally. Most interpreters understand it to mean that Christ was treated as sin itself, or identified with sinful humanity, in his death. A substantial minority note that the Septuagint sometimes uses this same word for the sin offering and read 'made him a sin offering'. The parallel with 'become the righteousness of God' favours leaving the plain word 'sin'.

verse.text: Working together with him, we also appeal to you not to receive the grace of God in vain.
verse.note: The Greek says only 'working together' and names no partner. Most translations supply 'with him' (God), because the previous sentence has God making his appeal through Paul, and that is followed here. The partner could instead be the Corinthians, or Paul's fellow workers.

verse.text: For he says, “At a favorable time I listened to you, and on a day of salvation I helped you.” Look, now is the truly favorable time; look, now is the day of salvation.

note.term: “At a favorable time I listened to you, and on a day of salvation I helped you.”

verse.note: The quotation is Isaiah 49:8 in its Greek form, where God addresses his Servant. In applying it, Paul replaces the quotation's word for 'favorable' with a stronger compound of the same word, rendered here 'truly favorable'.

verse.text: We give no cause for stumbling in anything, so that no fault may be found with our service,
verse.note: The noun belongs to the same word-family as 'servants' in the next verse, and 'service' keeps that link visible. 'Ministry', the usual rendering, now suggests a clerical office, whereas the Greek word means carrying out a task on someone's behalf. The Greek says simply 'the service'; 'our' is supplied for English.

verse.text: but in everything we commend ourselves as God’s servants: in great endurance, in afflictions, in hardships, in dire straits,
in beatings, in imprisonments, in riots, in hard labor, in sleepless nights, in hunger,
verse.note: The word normally means fasting as a religious practice. In a list of hardships that includes beatings, prisons and sleepless nights, most interpreters take it as going without food from necessity. Voluntary fasting remains possible.

verse.text: in purity, in knowledge, in patience, in kindness, in the Holy Spirit, in love without pretense,

note.traditional: by the Holy Ghost / the Holy Spirit

verse.note: The phrase stands without the article in a list of personal qualities, so some read it as 'in a spirit of holiness', a holy disposition. Most translations and commentators take it as the Holy Spirit, as here. The pairing with 'the power of God' in the next verse supports that reading.

verse.text: in the word of truth, in the power of God; with the weapons of righteousness for the right hand and the left,
verse.note: The Greek can mean the message that is true, that is, the gospel, as the same phrase does elsewhere in the Pauline letters. It can also mean 'truthful speech', a quality of Paul's own conduct. Translations are divided; the pairing with 'the power of God' slightly favors the first.

Greek has a single word-family where English has two: righteous and just, righteousness and justice, justify. The word covers being in the right, doing what is right, and God's action to set things right. Some scholars prefer 'justice' in English. Weapons 'for the right hand and the left' probably means a full kit, sword in the right hand for attack and shield in the left for defense.

verse.text: through honor and dishonor, through ill repute and good repute; as deceivers and yet true,
as unknown and yet well known, as dying, and look, we live; as disciplined and yet not put to death,

note.term: as disciplined and yet not put to death

verse.note: The wording echoes Psalm 118:18 (117:18 in the Greek numbering): 'The Lord disciplined me severely, but did not hand me over to death.' The preceding 'and look, we live' may echo the verse before it in the same psalm, 'I shall not die, but live.'

verse.text: as grieving yet always rejoicing, as poor yet making many rich, as having nothing and yet possessing everything.
We have spoken openly to you, Corinthians; our heart is opened wide.
You are not cramped for room in us; you are cramped in your own affections.
As a fair exchange—I speak as to children—open yourselves wide too.
Do not be yoked in a mismatched pair with unbelievers. For what partnership have righteousness and lawlessness, or what fellowship has light with darkness?
verse.note: The verb occurs only here in the New Testament. It recalls the Torah's ban on pairing animals of different kinds (Leviticus 19:19 in Greek uses the related adjective; compare Deuteronomy 22:10 on ploughing with an ox and a donkey together). The point is difference of kind, not inequality of rank, which 'unequally' can suggest. Paul does not say which partnerships he has in mind; marriage, business ties and involvement in pagan worship have all been proposed.

The passage from here to 7:1 interrupts Paul's appeal for open hearts, which resumes at 7:2, and it contains several words found nowhere else in his letters. Some scholars therefore think it is a fragment from another letter or a later insertion. No manuscript omits it, and many scholars defend it as Paul's own digression.

verse.text: What harmony has Christ with Beliar, or what share has a believer with an unbeliever?
verse.note: Beliar is a variant form of Belial, from a Hebrew word meaning 'worthlessness'. In Jewish writings of the period, including the Dead Sea Scrolls, it is a name for the chief adversary of God. This is its only occurrence in the New Testament.

verse.text: And what agreement has God’s temple with idols? For we are the temple of the living God, just as God said: “I will dwell among them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they will be my people.
verse.note: Many manuscripts read 'you are the temple of the living God'. The reading 'we are' has strong early support and is the more likely original. 'You are' probably arose under the influence of 1 Corinthians 3:16.

note.term: “I will dwell among them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they will be my people.

verse.note: Verses 16–18 weave several scriptural passages into one continuous quotation. They are Leviticus 26:11–12 with Ezekiel 37:27; Isaiah 52:11; Ezekiel 20:34 ('I will welcome you'); and 2 Samuel 7:14, widened to 'sons and daughters', perhaps under the influence of Isaiah 43:6. The wording is adapted freely, not cited exactly.

text.q: Therefore come out from among them and be separate, says the Lord, and touch nothing unclean; and I will welcome you,
and I will be a father to you, and you will be sons and daughters to me, says the Lord Almighty.”

verse.text: Since we have these promises, then, dear friends, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of body and spirit, bringing holiness to completion in the fear of God.
Make room for us. We wronged no one, we corrupted no one, we took advantage of no one.
verse.note: The verb means to make space or have room for something. Paul is resuming the appeal of 6:11-13, where he said his heart was wide open to the Corinthians and asked them to open wide in return. Many translations add 'in your hearts' to make the link explicit.

verse.text: I do not say this to condemn you, for I have said before that you are in our hearts, to die together and to live together.
Great is my frankness toward you; great is my boasting about you. I am filled with comfort; I am overflowing with joy in all our affliction.
verse.note: The Greek word covers both outspokenness and confidence. Some translations take it here as 'I have great confidence in you', which pairs well with the boasting that follows. The sense of open, unguarded speech is the more common one in the period and fits Paul's defence of his blunt earlier letter.

verse.text: For even when we came into Macedonia, our bodies had no relief; we were afflicted in every way—conflicts outside, fears within.
But God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the arrival of Titus,

note.traditional: comforteth those that are cast down

verse.note: The wording echoes the Greek version of Isaiah 49:13, where God is said to have comforted the lowly of his people. The word can mean 'humble' or 'lowly' in status; here the context of exhaustion and fear points to people brought low in spirit.

This is the word used elsewhere for the 'coming' of Christ. Its ordinary meaning is simply someone's arrival and resulting presence, and that is the sense here. Paul had been waiting anxiously for Titus to return from Corinth with news (2:12-13).

verse.text: and not only by his arrival but also by the comfort with which he was comforted over you, as he reported to us your longing, your mourning, your zeal for me, so that I rejoiced all the more.
For even if I grieved you with my letter, I do not regret it. Even if I did regret it (I see that that letter grieved you, though only for a while),
verse.note: This is the letter Paul says in 2:3-4 he wrote 'with many tears' after a painful episode at Corinth. Most scholars think it is lost. A minority identify it with 1 Corinthians or with chapters 10-13 of this letter.

The sentence is grammatically rough in Greek, and the manuscripts differ. Some add 'for' after 'I see', and a few read 'seeing'. The translation follows the shorter reading and treats the clause as a parenthesis. The overall sense is the same in each form.

verse.text: now I rejoice, not because you were grieved, but because you were grieved into turning back. For you were grieved in God's way, so that you might suffer no loss through us in anything.
verse.note: 'Repentance' in modern English suggests chiefly feeling sorry. Paul here distinguishes the grief from what it leads to, a change of direction toward God like the prophets' call to 'return'. Most translations keep 'repentance' as an established term understood to include a change of life.

note.traditional: after a godly manner; godly sorrow

verse.note: The Greek is literally 'according to God', repeated in verses 10 and 11. It means grief of the kind God approves or intends, as opposed to 'the world's grief'. The traditional 'godly sorrow' conveys much the same idea. Some translations render it 'as God intended'.

verse.text: For grief in God's way brings about a turning back that leads to salvation and leaves no regret, but the world's grief produces death.
verse.note: The adjective 'unregretted' could describe either the turning back or the salvation; the Greek grammar allows both. The translation leaves it attached to the whole outcome. The word picks up Paul's 'I do not regret it' in verse 8. It is a different Greek word from the one rendered 'turning back'.

verse.text: For see what earnestness this very thing, being grieved in God's way, has produced in you—and what a defense of yourselves, what indignation, what fear, what longing, what zeal, what punishment of the wrong! In every way you have shown yourselves to be innocent in the matter.
verse.note: The word means the carrying out of justice. It can refer to punishing an offender or to vindicating the injured party. Here it most likely refers to the congregation's disciplining of the offender (compare 2:6), though 'readiness to see justice done' is also a fair rendering.

verse.text: So then, even though I wrote to you, it was not on account of the one who did the wrong, nor on account of the one who was wronged, but so that your earnestness for us might be made plain to you before God.

note.term: the one who did the wrong
note.traditional: his cause that had done the wrong

verse.note: Paul does not name either party, and their identity is uncertain. The offender is usually linked with the person disciplined in 2:5-11, and many scholars think the one wronged was Paul himself or one of his associates. An older view connects the case with the man of 1 Corinthians 5.

verse.text: Because of this we have been comforted. And on top of our comfort, we rejoiced even more at the joy of Titus, because his spirit has been refreshed by all of you.
For if I have boasted to him about you in anything, I was not put to shame; but just as everything we said to you was true, so also our boasting before Titus has proved true.
And his affection for you is all the greater as he remembers the obedience of all of you, how you received him with fear and trembling.
I rejoice that in everything I have confidence in you.
We make known to you, brothers and sisters, the grace of God that has been given in the assemblies of Macedonia:
verse.note: The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and the Septuagint's word for Israel assembled. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. 'Assembly' is used throughout this translation so that the one Greek word is visible as one word.

A single Greek word, charis, runs through this chapter and ties it together: God's 'grace' (v. 1), the 'favor' of taking part (v. 4), the collection itself as an 'act of grace' (vv. 6, 7, 19), the 'grace' of Christ (v. 9) and 'thanks' to God (v. 16). English cannot keep one word for all of these, but a Greek reader heard Paul presenting the Corinthians' gift as a response in kind to what God had given.

The Greek plural, used to address a mixed community, was understood to include the women in it. Older translations have 'brethren' or 'brothers'; many recent ones use 'brothers and sisters'. Where the word refers to particular men, as in verses 18, 22 and 23, it is rendered 'brother' or 'brothers'.

verse.text: amid a severe test of affliction, their overflowing joy and their deep poverty overflowed into the wealth of their generosity.
verse.note: The word's basic sense is singleness or sincerity: giving with no ulterior motive and nothing held back. In contexts of giving, most translators and lexicons take it to shade into open-handedness, and that is followed here. Some scholars prefer 'sincerity' or 'single-minded devotion'.

verse.text: For according to their means, I testify, and beyond their means, they gave of their own accord,

note.term: they gave of their own accord
note.traditional: they gave of their own accord

verse.note: Paul's sentence in verses 3 to 5 has no main verb until 'they gave themselves' in verse 5; 'they gave' is supplied here, as in most translations, to make the English run. 'Of their own accord' could instead be attached to what follows: 'of their own accord they begged us'.

verse.text: begging us with much urging for the favor of sharing in the service to the holy ones—
verse.note: The word describes all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint's language for Israel. 'Saints' now suggests canonised individuals or people of exceptional virtue; some translations use 'God's people'. Here it refers to the believers in Jerusalem, for whom the collection was being raised.

verse.text: and not just as we had hoped, but they gave themselves first to the Lord and to us, through the will of God,
so that we urged Titus that, just as he had already made a beginning, so he should also complete this act of grace among you.
But just as you overflow in everything—in faith and speech and knowledge and all earnestness and the love from us that is in you—see that you overflow in this act of grace too.

note.term: the love from us that is in you

verse.note: The manuscripts are divided between 'the love from us in you' and 'the love from you in us', which would mean 'your love for us'. The text translated here follows the first reading, which is the harder one and is adopted by the main critical editions; many translations follow the second.

verse.text: I am not saying this as a command; rather, through the earnestness of others I am testing the genuineness of your love as well.
For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ: that though he was rich, for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich.
And in this matter I am giving my opinion, for this is to your advantage, you who since last year had already made a beginning not only in doing but also in wanting to.
Now complete the doing as well, so that your eagerness in wanting may be matched by your completing it, out of what you have.
For if the eagerness is there, it is acceptable according to what one has, not according to what one does not have.
For this is not so that others may have relief and you affliction, but as a matter of equality:
at the present time your surplus supplies their lack, so that their surplus may in turn supply your lack, and so there may be equality,
as it is written: “The one who had much did not have too much, and the one who had little did not have too little.”

note.term: “The one who had much did not have too much, and the one who had little did not have too little.”

verse.note: The quotation is from Exodus 16:18, about the manna in the wilderness: however much or little each person gathered, everyone ended up with enough. Paul uses it as a picture of resources evened out among God's people.

verse.text: But thanks be to God, who puts the same earnestness for you into the heart of Titus,
for he accepted our urging, and, being more earnest still, he is setting out to you of his own accord.
verse.note: The Greek verbs here and in verses 18 and 22 ('we are sending') are past tenses. Most interpreters take them as the letter-writer's convention of adopting the reader's point of view, since Titus and the brothers probably carried this letter; hence the English present. It is possible, though less likely, that they had already left.

verse.text: With him we are sending the brother whose praise in the good news has spread through all the assemblies—
verse.note: The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news. 'Gospel' has become a religious term and a book title, so 'good news' is used throughout this translation; many modern versions alternate between the two.

Paul does not name this brother or the one in verse 22, presumably because the Corinthians would meet them when the letter arrived. Guesses since antiquity have included Luke, Barnabas and others, but his identity is unknown.

verse.text: and not only that, but he has also been chosen by the assemblies as our traveling companion with this act of grace that is being administered by us, for the glory of the Lord himself and to show our eagerness—
we are taking this precaution so that no one may find fault with us over this lavish gift that is being administered by us,
for we give thought to what is honorable not only before the Lord but also before people.
And with them we are sending our brother, whom we have often tested in many matters and found earnest, and who is now much more earnest because of his great confidence in you.
As for Titus, he is my partner and fellow worker for you; as for our brothers, they are envoys of the assemblies, the glory of Christ.
verse.note: The Greek word is the one elsewhere translated 'apostles'. Here it has its ordinary sense of people sent as authorised representatives, in this case by the assemblies, to accompany the collection. Most translations use 'messengers' or 'representatives'; 'envoys' conveys that they carry delegated authority.

verse.text: So show them the proof of your love and of our boasting about you, in full view of the assemblies.
For as to the service for the holy ones, it is superfluous for me to write to you,
verse.note: The Greek word is an ordinary term for service rendered or a task carried out on someone's behalf; 'ministry' now suggests a church office or profession. Here it refers to the collection of money Paul was organising among his largely non-Jewish congregations for the impoverished believers in Jerusalem, the subject of chapters 8 and 9.

The traditional 'saints' now suggests canonised individuals or people of exceptional virtue. Paul uses the word for all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint's language for Israel; here it means specifically the believers in Jerusalem. Many translations keep 'saints'; others use 'God's people'.

verse.text: for I know your eagerness, which I boast about on your behalf to the Macedonians, saying that Achaia has been ready since last year; and your zeal has stirred up most of them.
But I am sending the brothers so that our boast about you may not prove empty in this matter, so that you may be ready, just as I kept saying you would be;
otherwise, if any Macedonians come with me and find you unprepared, we—not to mention you—would be put to shame in this undertaking.
verse.note: Older translations, and several current ones, render this 'in this confidence' or 'for being so confident'. The standard modern lexicon argues that the sense 'confidence' is not securely attested for this word in the period, and that it means here a plan, project or undertaking (or, on another view, 'situation'). Some recent translations already read 'undertaking'; the matter remains disputed.

verse.text: So I thought it necessary to urge the brothers to go on ahead to you and prepare in advance the bounty you promised beforehand, so that it may be ready as a bounty and not as something extorted.
verse.note: The Greek word normally means 'blessing' and is used here for a gift given freely and generously. The same word returns in verse 6, literally 'sows on the basis of blessings', which is why 'bounty' and 'bountifully' are used to keep Paul's link between the two verses.

The word means greed, the desire to have more. It may refer to greed on the collectors' side, so that the gift would look like money squeezed out of the Corinthians (the reading followed here), or to a grasping spirit in the givers, yielding 'not as something grudgingly given'. Both readings have scholarly support.

verse.text: The point is this: whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully.
Each of you should give as you have decided in your heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.
verse.note: This echoes a line found in the Greek version of Proverbs 22:8 but absent from the Hebrew text: 'God blesses a cheerful and giving man.' That same verse of Proverbs speaks of sowing and reaping, the image Paul has just used.

verse.text: And God is able to make all grace overflow to you, so that, having all you need in all things at all times, you may overflow in every good work.
As it is written: “He has scattered abroad, he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever.”
verse.note: Greek has one word-family where English has two (righteous/just, righteousness/justice). The quotation is from Psalm 112:9, where the one who gives to the poor is the person who fears the Lord, and 'righteousness' is right conduct shown in generosity; in Jewish usage of the period the word could come close to meaning charitable giving. Some interpreters think Paul takes God as the subject of the quotation.

verse.text: Now the one who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your seed and increase the harvest of your righteousness.
You will be enriched in every way for every kind of generosity, which through us produces thanksgiving to God,
verse.note: The word's basic sense is singleness or sincerity: giving without reserve or ulterior motive. Most translations render it 'generosity' here and in verse 13 because of the context, but some lexicographers hold that 'sincere, wholehearted concern' is sufficient in every occurrence. The difference is one of emphasis: the open spirit of the giving versus its amount.

verse.text: because the service of this public offering is not only supplying what the holy ones lack but is also overflowing through many thanksgivings to God.
verse.note: Traditional versions have 'the administration (or ministry) of this service', which blurs two different Greek words. This one was the term in Greek cities for a public service that a citizen undertook at his own expense, and in the Septuagint for the service of priests in the sanctuary. Paul presents the collection as both a civic-style benefaction and an act of worship; 'public offering' attempts to carry both.

verse.text: Through the proof this service gives, they will glorify God for the obedience that comes with your confession of the good news of Christ and for the generosity of your sharing with them and with everyone,
verse.note: The Greek has only a participle, 'glorifying God', with no stated subject. Most interpreters take the recipients in Jerusalem as those who praise God because of the Corinthians' obedience, which fits verse 14; others take the Corinthians as the subject ('you glorify God by your obedience'). The grammar of verses 11–14 is loose and allows either.

'Gospel' has become a religious term or the name of a kind of book. The Greek was an ordinary word for an announcement of good news, used also of public and imperial proclamations. Many modern translations alternate between 'gospel' and 'good news'.

verse.text: and in their prayer for you they long for you because of the surpassing grace of God upon you.
Thanks be to God for his indescribable gift!
verse.note: The word translated 'Thanks' is the same Greek word translated 'grace' in verses 8 and 14; it covers both a favour freely given and the gratitude it calls forth. Paul closes the whole discussion of the collection, in which this word has recurred throughout chapters 8 and 9, by returning grace to God as thanks.

verse.text: Now I, Paul, appeal to you myself, by the gentleness and forbearance of Christ—I who am lowly when face to face among you, but bold toward you when away.
verse.note: The traditional 'meekness' now suggests weakness or timidity, which the Greek word does not. It describes a gentle, unassertive manner, and 'gentleness' is the mainstream modern rendering. The paired word, rendered 'forbearance', was often used of the leniency of someone with the power to be severe.

Paul appears to be echoing a charge made by his critics in Corinth (see verse 10): that he is unimpressive and submissive in person and bold only from a distance. In ordinary Greek usage the word was often unflattering, meaning low in status or servile.

verse.text: I beg you that when I am present I may not have to be bold with the confidence I reckon on daring to use against certain people, who reckon that we walk according to the flesh.
verse.note: Paul plays on two phrases. To walk 'in the flesh' (verse 3) is simply to live as an ordinary mortal human being. To walk or wage war 'according to the flesh' is to act by merely human standards and motives. 'Walk' is a Semitic idiom for how one conducts one's life.

verse.text: For though we walk in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh—
for the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh but powerful through God for the tearing down of strongholds—we tear down reasonings
verse.note: The Greek is literally 'powerful to God', and its force is disputed. It may mean powerful by God's enabling (as rendered here), powerful in God's service, powerful in God's sight, or it may be a Semitic idiom meaning 'supremely powerful'. Translations and commentators are divided.

Verses 4–6 follow the sequence of an ancient siege: fortifications are torn down, raised defences are levelled, the defenders are taken captive, and remaining resistance is punished. Paul applies the picture to arguments and ways of thinking opposed to the knowledge of God.

verse.text: and every high thing raised up against the knowledge of God, and we take every thought captive into obedience to Christ,
and we stand ready to punish every disobedience, once your obedience is complete.
Look at what is right in front of your face. If anyone is confident in himself that he belongs to Christ, let him reckon this again for himself: just as he belongs to Christ, so also do we.

note.term: Look at what is right in front of your face.
note.traditional: Do ye look on things after the outward appearance?

verse.note: The Greek verb form can be a command ('Look at what is in front of you'), a statement ('You are looking only at the surface of things') or a question. Many modern translations take it as a command, as here; others take it as a rebuke for judging by appearances. The phrase 'in front of your face' picks up 'face to face' in verse 1.

verse.text: For even if I boast somewhat more about our authority, which the Lord gave for building you up and not for tearing you down, I will not be put to shame.
I do not want to seem as though I were trying to frighten you through my letters.
For “His letters,” someone says, “are weighty and strong, but his bodily presence is weak and his speech counts for nothing.”
verse.note: The Greek verb is singular, 'he says' or 'one says'. It may refer to a particular critic or be an impersonal way of reporting what is generally being said; some manuscripts have the plural 'they say'. 'Such a person' in verse 11 is equally open to either reading.

verse.text: Let such a person reckon this: what we are in word through letters when absent, we also are in deed when present.

For we do not dare to class or compare ourselves with some of those who commend themselves. But when they measure themselves by themselves and compare themselves with themselves, they are without understanding.
verse.note: A few manuscripts of the Western tradition lack these words and the opening 'We, however' of verse 13. In that form of the text it is Paul and his colleagues who measure themselves by their own standard. The longer reading translated here is much better attested and is followed by nearly all editions.

verse.text: We, however, will not boast beyond measure, but according to the measure of the sphere that God apportioned to us as our measure, to reach even as far as you—
verse.note: The Greek word basically means a measuring rod, and hence a standard or limit. Here and in verses 15–16 most interpreters take it to mean the area of mission work God marked out for Paul, which is why it is rendered 'sphere'. Others understand it as the standard by which his work is to be assessed. The sentence is compressed and its exact sense is debated.

verse.text: for we are not overstretching ourselves, as though we did not reach you, since we came even as far as you with the good news of Christ—
verse.note: 'Gospel' has become a religious term or the name of a kind of book. The Greek was an ordinary word for an announcement of good news, including public proclamations. Many modern translations alternate between 'gospel' and 'good news'; the related verb in verse 16 is rendered 'proclaim the good news'.

verse.text: we do not boast beyond measure in the labors of others, but we have hope that, as your faith grows, we will be greatly enlarged among you in keeping with our sphere,
so as to proclaim the good news in the regions beyond you, and not to boast in what is already done in another's sphere.
But, “Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.”

note.term: “Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.”

verse.note: This is a condensed quotation of Jeremiah 9:24 (9:23 in the Septuagint), where the one who boasts is told to boast in understanding and knowing the Lord. Paul gives no introductory formula here, but he cites the same words with 'as it is written' in 1 Corinthians 1:31.

verse.text: For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends.
I wish you would put up with a little foolishness from me. But in fact you are putting up with me.

note.term: you are putting up with me

verse.note: The Greek verb form can be either a statement ('you are putting up with me') or a command ('do put up with me'). Many translations choose the command. The statement is taken here because the preceding wish is phrased as something not yet happening, which the 'but in fact' then corrects; either reading is defensible.

verse.text: For I am jealous for you with God's own jealousy, since I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ.
But I am afraid that somehow, as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, your minds may be corrupted and turned from single-minded and pure devotion to Christ.
verse.note: Some manuscripts lack the words 'and the purity', reading only 'from the single-mindedness that is toward Christ'. The longer reading has strong early support and is printed in the SBLGNT, but the words could have dropped out or been added by accident because the two Greek nouns end alike. The word rendered 'single-minded' is often translated 'simplicity' or 'sincerity'; it denotes undivided loyalty.

verse.text: For if someone comes and proclaims another Jesus, whom we did not proclaim, or you receive a different spirit, which you did not receive, or different good news, which you did not accept, you put up with it well enough.
verse.note: The Greek word was an ordinary term for a welcome announcement, and the related verb in verse 7 ('proclaimed ... good news') shares its root. 'Gospel' is the customary English and is not wrong, but it now suggests a book or a genre. Several modern translations also use 'good news'.

verse.text: For I reckon that I fall short of those super-apostles in nothing.
verse.note: Paul's phrase is literally 'the exceedingly-beyond apostles', and the same expression recurs at 12:11. Most scholars take it as sarcasm aimed at the rival missionaries in Corinth, whom he calls false apostles in verse 13. A minority think it refers, without sarcasm, to the leading apostles in Jerusalem, to whom the rivals appealed.

verse.text: Even if I am untrained in speaking, I am not so in knowledge; in every way we have made this plain to you in all things.
Or did I commit a sin by humbling myself so that you might be exalted, because I proclaimed God's good news to you free of charge?
I robbed other assemblies, taking pay from them so as to serve you,
verse.note: The Greek word meant a gathering of people: a city's citizen assembly, and in the Greek Old Testament the assembled people of Israel. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. 'Assembly' is used throughout this translation so that the one Greek word is always visible.

verse.text: and when I was with you and ran short, I was a burden to no one, for the brothers who came from Macedonia made up my shortfall. In everything I kept myself from weighing on you, and I will keep doing so.
As the truth of Christ is in me, this boast of mine will not be silenced in the regions of Achaia.
Why? Because I do not love you? God knows I do.
What I am doing I will go on doing, so as to cut off the opportunity from those who want an opportunity to be found on the same footing as we are in what they boast about.
For such people are false apostles, deceitful workers, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ.
And no wonder, for Satan himself disguises himself as an angel of light.
So it is no great thing if his servants also disguise themselves as servants of righteousness. Their end will be according to their works.
verse.note: Greek has a single word-family where English has two: righteous and just, righteousness and justice, justify. The traditional 'righteousness' is kept here, but the reader should hear in it both doing what is right and being in the right.

verse.text: I say again, let no one think me a fool. But if you do, then accept me even as a fool, so that I too may boast a little.
What I am saying I am not saying according to the Lord, but as in foolishness, in this undertaking of boasting.
verse.note: Most translations render this 'confidence of boasting'. The sense 'confidence' is thinly attested for this word in the period, and recent lexical work favours 'project, undertaking' or 'situation' here and at 9:4. The matter remains disputed, and the traditional rendering is still widely defended.

verse.text: Since many boast according to the flesh, I too will boast.
For you gladly put up with fools, wise as you are!
For you put up with it if someone enslaves you, if someone devours you, if someone takes advantage of you, if someone exalts himself, if someone strikes you in the face.
To my shame I say it: we were too weak for that! But wherever anyone else is daring (I am speaking in foolishness), I am daring too.
Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they Abraham's offspring? So am I.
Are they servants of Christ? I am talking like a madman: I am more so. In labors far more, in prisons far more, in beatings beyond measure, in danger of death often.
Five times I received from Jews the forty lashes less one.
verse.note: Deuteronomy 25:3 limits a flogging to forty strokes. Jewish practice stopped at thirty-nine so that a miscount could not break the law. This was a synagogue punishment, which means Paul kept submitting to synagogue discipline as a Jew. None of the five occasions is recorded in Acts.

verse.text: Three times I was beaten with rods, once I was stoned, three times I was shipwrecked; a night and a day I have spent adrift on the open sea.
verse.note: Beating with rods was a punishment ordered by Roman magistrates, as distinct from the synagogue lashes of verse 24. Acts 16:22-23 records one instance, at Philippi. Roman citizens were legally exempt from it, though the exemption was not always honoured.

verse.text: On journeys often, in dangers from rivers, dangers from bandits, dangers from my own people, dangers from Gentiles, dangers in the city, dangers in the wilderness, dangers at sea, dangers among false brothers;
verse.note: The Greek word means 'peoples' or 'nations'. In the plural, in Jewish usage, it means the non-Jewish peoples. This translation uses 'Gentiles' for the latter sense and 'nations' for the former; they are the same Greek word. Here it stands opposite 'my own people', that is, fellow Jews.

verse.text: in labor and toil, in sleepless nights often, in hunger and thirst, often without food, in cold and without enough clothing.
Apart from other things, there is the daily pressure on me, my anxiety for all the assemblies.

note.traditional: Beside those things that are without

verse.note: The phrase can mean 'apart from the things left unmentioned' or 'apart from external things', that is, the outward hardships just listed. The first is the more common view today and is followed here. The word rendered 'pressure' also has a manuscript variant, and its sense ranges from 'pressure' to 'attention' or 'what comes upon me'; the general meaning is not affected.

verse.text: Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn?
If boasting is necessary, I will boast of the things that show my weakness.
The God and Father of the Lord Jesus, he who is blessed forever, knows that I am not lying.
In Damascus the governor under King Aretas was guarding the city of the Damascenes in order to seize me,

note.traditional: the governor under Aretas the king

verse.note: Aretas IV ruled the Nabataean kingdom, south and east of Judea, until about AD 40, which makes this one of the few fixed points for dating Paul's life. The official's title is 'ethnarch'. Whether he governed Damascus for Aretas or was the head of the Nabataean community there is disputed. Acts 9:23-25 tells the same escape.

verse.text: and I was lowered in a basket through a window in the wall and escaped his hands.
I must boast; there is nothing to be gained by it, but I will go on to visions and revelations of the Lord.
I know a man in Christ who fourteen years ago—whether in the body I do not know, or outside the body I do not know; God knows—was snatched away as far as the third heaven.
verse.note: Almost all interpreters agree that Paul is describing his own experience in the third person; verse 7 makes this plain when the revelations turn out to be his. The indirection lets him report the vision without making it a boast about himself. Fourteen years before this letter would fall in the early 40s, a period of his life about which little else is known.

The verb means to seize or carry off suddenly and by force; it is used of robbers and of wild animals as well as of being taken to heaven. “Caught up” is the usual rendering and is not wrong, but “snatched away” keeps the abruptness and the sense that the man did nothing to bring it about. The same word and rendering recur in verse 4.

Jewish writings of the period speak of several heavens stacked one above another, sometimes three and sometimes seven. Most scholars think Paul means the highest, and that “paradise” in verse 4 names the same place rather than a further stage. “Paradise” was the Septuagint’s word for the garden of Eden and had come to mean the blessed place in God’s presence.

verse.text: And I know that such a man—whether in the body or apart from the body I do not know; God knows—
was snatched away into paradise and heard unutterable words, which no human being is permitted to speak.
On behalf of such a man I will boast, but on my own behalf I will not boast, except in my weaknesses.
For if I should want to boast, I will not be a fool, for I will be speaking the truth. But I refrain, so that no one will credit me with more than what they see in me or hear from me,

even given the extraordinary character of the revelations. Therefore, so that I would not become conceited, a thorn in the flesh was given to me, a messenger of Satan to beat me, so that I would not become conceited.

note.term: even given the extraordinary character of the revelations
note.traditional: And lest I should be exalted above measure through the abundance of the revelations

verse.note: The edition translated here attaches this phrase to the end of the sentence in verse 6 and begins a new sentence with “Therefore”. Some manuscripts lack “therefore”, and many translations then join the phrase to what follows: “And because of the extraordinary revelations, to keep me from becoming conceited, a thorn was given me.” The grammar is rough on either reading and the connection is disputed.

The Greek word can mean a pointed stake, but in the Septuagint and everyday usage of the period it usually means a thorn or splinter. What Paul refers to is unknown: a chronic illness or bodily affliction is the commonest suggestion, and persistent opponents or persecution is another. The phrase “messenger of Satan” could equally be translated “angel of Satan”, since the Greek word covers both.

verse.text: Three times I pleaded with the Lord about this, that it would leave me.

And he has said to me, “My grace is enough for you, for power is brought to completion in weakness.” So I will most gladly boast in my weaknesses instead, so that the power of Christ may make its dwelling upon me.
verse.note: The verb means to finish, accomplish or bring to its goal. “Made perfect” is the traditional rendering, but “perfect” now suggests flawlessness, whereas the point is that power reaches its full effect where there is weakness. Most translations keep “made perfect”.

This rare verb means to take up quarters or come to dwell in or over a place. Many scholars hear an echo of the Septuagint’s language for God’s presence dwelling in the tabernacle, though that is not certain. “Rest upon” is the usual English rendering and loses the image of taking up residence.

verse.text: That is why I am content in weaknesses, in insults, in hardships, in persecutions and distresses, for Christ’s sake; for when I am weak, then I am powerful.
verse.note: The adjective is from the same word family as “power” in verse 9, and Paul is completing that thought: Christ’s power dwells on him in his weakness. “Then I am strong” is the familiar rendering and is equally accurate as English; “powerful” is used here so that the link with verse 9 can be heard.

verse.text: I have become a fool; you forced me to it. For I ought to have been commended by you, since I was in no way inferior to the super-apostles, even if I am nothing.
verse.note: The phrase combines “apostles” with an adverb meaning “exceedingly, beyond measure”. Most scholars take it as Paul’s sarcastic label for the rival missionaries who had come to Corinth; a minority think he means the leading apostles in Jerusalem, in which case the tone is not mocking. The same phrase occurs in 11:5.

verse.text: The signs of an apostle were indeed worked among you with all endurance, by signs and wonders and acts of power.
For in what way were you made worse off than the rest of the assemblies, except that I myself was not a burden to you? Forgive me this wrong!
verse.note: The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and the Septuagint’s word for Israel assembled before God. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. This translation uses “assembly” throughout so that the one Greek word is recognisable everywhere.

verse.text: Look, I am ready to come to you this third time, and I will not be a burden; for I am not seeking what is yours, but you. For children ought not to save up for their parents, but parents for their children.
And I will most gladly spend and be utterly spent for your lives. If I love you more, am I loved less?
verse.note: The Greek word means a person’s life or self, and “for your lives” here amounts to “for you”, as several modern translations render it. “Souls” is the older rendering, but it suggests to a modern reader an immaterial part of the person as distinct from the body, which is not the point here.

verse.text: But granted, I did not weigh you down; yet, crafty fellow that I am, I took you in by deceit.

note.term: crafty fellow that I am, I took you in by deceit
note.traditional: being crafty, I caught you with guile

verse.note: Paul is not confessing; he is voicing, with irony, a charge made against him. The suspicion seems to have been that although he took no support for himself, he was getting at the Corinthians’ money indirectly through his associates and the collection for Jerusalem. Verses 17 and 18 answer that charge.

verse.text: Surely I did not take advantage of you through any of those I have sent to you?
I urged Titus to go, and I sent the brother with him. Titus did not take advantage of you, did he? Did we not walk in the same spirit? Not in the same footsteps?
Have you been thinking all this time that we are defending ourselves to you? It is before God, in Christ, that we speak; and all of it, beloved, is for building you up.
