For I am afraid that somehow when I come I may find you not as I wish, and that I may be found by you not as you wish; that somehow there may be strife, jealousy, outbursts of anger, selfish rivalries, slander, gossip, arrogance and disorder.

I am afraid that when I come again my God may humble me before you, and I may mourn over many of those who sinned earlier and have not turned back from the impurity, sexual immorality and debauchery that they practised.
verse.note: The word “again” can be taken with the coming, as here, or with the humbling: “that when I come my God may again humble me before you.” The second reading would allude to an earlier painful visit (compare 2:1). The word order allows either and scholars are divided.

The traditional rendering is “repented”, which most translations keep as an established term. In current English “repent” centres on feeling sorry, whereas the Greek word, shaped by the prophets’ call to return to God, means a change of direction in mind and conduct. This translation uses “turn back” throughout.

verse.text: This is the third time I am coming to you. “Every matter shall be established by the mouth of two or three witnesses.”

note.term: by the mouth of two or three witnesses

verse.note: Paul quotes the rule of evidence in Deuteronomy 19:15, which required at least two witnesses to sustain a charge. Many interpreters think he is treating his visits, or his repeated warnings, as the required witnesses against the offenders. Others take it as notice that he will hold a formal hearing when he arrives. The Greek does not settle which.

verse.text: I have said it before, and I say it in advance now, as I did when present the second time and do now while absent, to those who sinned before and to all the rest: if I come again, I will spare no one,
since you are seeking proof that Christ is speaking in me. He is not weak toward you but is powerful among you.
For indeed he was crucified in weakness, but he lives by the power of God. And we too are weak in him, but we will live with him by the power of God toward you.

note.term: we will live with him by the power of God toward you

verse.note: The future 'we will live' could refer to the resurrection. The closing words 'toward you' suggest instead that Paul means his coming visit, when he will act with Christ's power in dealing with the Corinthians. Most commentators take it this way. Some manuscripts read 'weak with him' instead of 'weak in him'.

verse.text: Examine yourselves to see whether you are in the faith; test yourselves. Or do you not recognize about yourselves that Jesus Christ is in you? Unless, of course, you fail the test.
verse.note: Verses 3 to 7 play on one Greek word family: 'proof' in verse 3, 'test yourselves', and 'fail' or 'pass the test' all share a root used of assaying metals and vetting candidates. The Corinthians demanded proof from Paul, and he turns the test back on them. Older versions have 'reprobates' or 'disqualified' here, which hides the link.

The same Greek phrase is rendered 'among you' in verse 3. Because 'you' is plural, it can mean either within each of you or among you as a community. 'In you' is the usual rendering here because the call to self-examination is personal, but the communal sense is equally possible.

verse.text: But I hope you will come to know that we do not fail the test.
We pray to God that you do nothing wrong, not so that we may be seen to pass the test, but so that you may do what is right, even if we should seem to fail it.
For we have no power against the truth, but only for the truth.
For we rejoice whenever we are weak and you are powerful. This is also what we pray for: your restoration.
verse.note: The noun and its verb in verse 11 were used of setting a bone, mending nets and putting something back into working order. 'Perfection' (KJV) suggests moral flawlessness, which is not the point. Paul wants a damaged community put right. Several modern versions also have 'restoration'; others have 'be made complete'.

verse.text: This is why I write these things while absent, so that when present I need not deal severely with you, in keeping with the authority the Lord gave me for building up and not for tearing down.
Finally, brothers and sisters, rejoice, be restored, be encouraged, be of one mind, live in peace, and the God of love and peace will be with you.
verse.note: The Greek plural was the normal way to address a mixed group of men and women, and Paul is writing to the whole congregation. 'Brothers' alone would now suggest men only. Many recent translations make the same choice.

The verb was also the ordinary Greek word for 'goodbye', and some translations render it 'farewell' here. 'Rejoice' is chosen because the same verb clearly has that meaning in verse 9 and it heads a list of commands. The next verb, rendered 'be encouraged', could also mean 'heed my appeal'.

verse.text: Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the holy ones greet you.
verse.note: 'Saints' now suggests canonised individuals or people of unusual virtue. Paul uses the word of all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint's language for Israel. Many translations keep 'saints'; others use 'God's people'.

verse.text: The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with all of you.

note.term: the fellowship of the Holy Spirit
note.traditional: the communion of the Holy Ghost

verse.note: The Greek can mean the fellowship the Spirit creates among believers, or a shared participation in the Spirit himself. Scholars are divided, and Paul may intend both. 'Fellowship of' leaves the question open as the Greek does.

note.term: The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ

verse.note: Many English Bibles divide verse 12 in two, so that this blessing is numbered verse 14. The wording is the same; only the numbering differs. The Greek has no verb, and 'be' is supplied in English.
